- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.5) and forecast is flat or declining, increase forecast slightly to capture bullish momentum.  
- After a sharp price spike, model tends to overshoot — cap forecast growth to 1–2% per day post-spike.  
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80), reduce forecast by 1–3% per day to align with reversion bias.  
- If history shows volatility clustering (e.g., 3+ consecutive high/low swings), model over-smooths — introduce 1–2% jitter in forecast to reflect volatility.  
- For long horizons (e.g., 30d), if true outcome shows late-period divergence (e.g., >90 after 20d), adjust forecast to reflect tail risk — add 1–3% downward bias in final 5–7 days.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 values, model tends to underreact — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day to compensate for muted sentiment.  
- When true outcome shows sudden upward jump (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often lags — adjust forecast to match true outcome 1–2 days ahead.
